subject: ela
skillName: Use technology to produce and publish writing
description: Students use technology, including the Internet, to produce, publish, and share writing and to interact and collaborate with others. They choose the right digital tool for a writing purpose (word processor, email, shared document, blog, or comment thread), apply formatting and editing features to improve a draft, give and respond to collaborative feedback respectfully and usefully, evaluate and credit online sources, follow safe and responsible online conduct, and demonstrate keyboarding skills sufficient to type a multi-page piece in a single sitting. Because this is a writing and technology standard rather than a reading standard, every item embeds the full prompt, message, comment, draft excerpt, or screen description it depends on inside the item itself, so the student needs nothing external and no live device. Items test the components through identification, selection, and short construction rather than full multi-page typing tasks. No math is involved.
subSkills: Choose the appropriate digital tool for a given writing purpose and audience (word processor for a report, email for a formal request, shared document for group work, blog or post for publishing to readers)
Apply word-processing and formatting features to improve writing (headings, bold and italics, bullet lists, spell check, find and replace, inserting a link or image with a caption)
Use editing and revision tools responsibly, recognizing that spell check and autocorrect can miss or introduce errors that the writer must catch
Collaborate on a shared document by leaving and responding to comments and suggestions that are specific, kind, and focused on improving the writing
Give and receive feedback using clear, respectful, on-topic language rather than vague praise or unkind remarks
Evaluate the credibility of an online source and cite or credit digital sources to avoid plagiarism
Follow safe and responsible online behavior when producing and publishing writing (protecting personal information, using respectful tone, respecting others' work)
Recognize that keyboarding fluency lets a writer type a multi-page piece in a single sitting, and identify good keyboarding and typing habits

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the right digital tool
problemArchetypes.example: Read the task in the item: 'You need to send a polite request to the school principal asking to start a recycling club.' Which digital tool fits this purpose best? Options: a group text to friends, a formal email, a public blog post, a private journal app. Answer: a formal email, because it reaches one specific reader directly and supports a respectful, formal tone.

problemArchetypes.name: Apply the right formatting feature
problemArchetypes.example: Read the goal embedded in the item: 'You want the three main sections of your report to stand out so readers can find them quickly.' Which word-processing feature best accomplishes this? Options: changing the font color of every word, adding headings to each section, making the whole document italic, increasing the page margins. Answer: adding headings, because headings label and separate the sections so readers can scan the report.

problemArchetypes.name: Catch the error spell check misses
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence embedded in the item: 'The principle of our school read the announcement.' Spell check shows no spelling errors. Which word is still wrong and what should it be? Answer: 'principle' should be 'principal,' because spell check accepts a correctly spelled word even when it is the wrong word for the meaning.

problemArchetypes.name: Write or choose a useful collaborative comment
problemArchetypes.example: Read the comment a student left on a classmate's shared draft: 'This part is bad.' Which revised comment gives feedback that is specific, kind, and useful? Options: 'I do not like it,' 'Great job, no changes,' 'Your second paragraph is clear, but the third one needs an example to support the point,' 'Why did you even write this?' Answer: the third option, because it points to a specific part, stays respectful, and suggests a concrete improvement.

problemArchetypes.name: Respond to feedback or a comment respectfully
problemArchetypes.example: Read the comment on a shared document embedded in the item: 'Could you add a source for this statistic?' Which is the best collaborative response? Options: deleting the comment without replying, replying 'Stop telling me what to do,' replying 'Good point, I will add the link to the study,' ignoring it. Answer: the third option, because it accepts useful feedback and states a clear next step.

problemArchetypes.name: Judge a source or credit it
problemArchetypes.example: Read the situation in the item: 'You found a helpful fact for your report on a website.' What is the responsible way to use it? Options: copy the sentences word for word with no mention of the site, put the fact in your own words and name the source, change a few words and claim it as your own, say a friend told you. Answer: put the fact in your own words and name the source, because crediting the source avoids plagiarism.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose safe and responsible online conduct
problemArchetypes.example: Read the scenario embedded in the item: 'You are about to publish your essay on the class blog.' Which choice shows safe, responsible online behavior? Options: include your home address and phone number, use a respectful tone and leave out private personal details, post an unkind comment about a classmate, share a friend's password. Answer: use a respectful tone and leave out private personal details, because protecting personal information and respecting others keeps publishing safe.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify good keyboarding habits
problemArchetypes.example: Read the goal in the item: 'You want to type a three-page story in one sitting without your hands getting tired.' Which habit best supports steady, accurate keyboarding? Options: looking at the keys and typing with one finger, resting fingers on the home row and keeping a steady rhythm, hitting keys as hard as possible, stopping after every word to reread. Answer: resting fingers on the home row and keeping a steady rhythm, because home-row touch typing builds the speed and stamina to type several pages at once.

Easy.description: A single short task statement, sentence, or one-line message (roughly 10 to 25 words) embedded in the item, with a clearly stated purpose. The task is identify-level: pick the obvious right tool, name a single formatting feature, choose the clearly polite comment, or select the safe online choice. Only one component is tested and the correct answer is unmistakable, with distractors that are clearly wrong.
constraints: Stimulus is one short sentence, task statement, or one-line message included in the prompt
Tests exactly one component (tool choice, one feature, one clear comment, one safety rule)
Identify-level task: select or label, no construction required
Distractors are clearly weaker (an obviously wrong tool, an unkind or off-topic comment, an unsafe action)

Medium.description: A short scenario, a two to three line message or comment thread, or a brief draft excerpt (roughly 30 to 60 words) embedded in the item. The task is analyze-level: match the best tool or feature when more than one is plausible, decide which collaborative comment is both specific and respectful, catch a real-word error that spell check would miss, or choose the most responsible way to credit a source. The student must weigh options that are partly defensible.
constraints: Stimulus is a short scenario, a brief comment exchange, or a sentence-level draft excerpt in the prompt
Tests feature choice in context, comment quality, source crediting, or a spell-check blind spot
Analyze-level task: choose or revise based on how well the option fits the purpose and audience
Distractors are plausible partial fits (a feature that helps a little, a comment that is kind but vague, a tool that could work but fits worse)

Hard.description: A multi-sentence scenario, a short collaborative thread with several comments, or a draft excerpt with more than one issue (roughly 60 to 110 words) embedded in the item. The task is evaluate-level: judge which response to feedback best moves the writing forward, decide which combination of tool and formatting choices best serves a stated audience and purpose, determine why a source is or is not credible and how to credit it, or choose the revision that most improves a draft across several digital-writing concerns at once. Requires inference about purpose, audience, and how the choices fit together.
constraints: Stimulus is a multi-sentence scenario, a multi-comment thread, or a draft excerpt with several issues in the prompt
Tests how multiple components interact: tool choice, formatting, collaboration, sourcing, and safe conduct
Evaluate-level task: select the best full response, revision, or set of choices and justify it against the purpose and audience
Requires inference to judge fit, credibility, and whether the choice best serves the reader and the writer

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student picks a digital tool by familiarity or popularity rather than by purpose and audience
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses a group text or social post to send a formal request to the principal instead of a formal email

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats formatting as decoration, choosing a feature that changes appearance but does not serve the writing goal
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects 'change the font color of every word' or 'make the document italic' to organize a report instead of adding headings

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student trusts spell check and autocorrect completely, assuming a document with no flagged words has no errors
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Says the sentence is correct because spell check found nothing, missing a real-word error such as 'principle' used for 'principal' or 'there' for 'their'

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks helpful feedback means vague praise or harsh judgment rather than specific, respectful, actionable comments
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses 'Great job, no changes' or 'This part is bad' instead of a comment that names a specific part and suggests an improvement

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student reacts to feedback defensively or dismissively instead of using it to improve the writing
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks 'Stop telling me what to do' or deleting the comment instead of accepting a useful suggestion and stating a next step

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student copies online text or facts without crediting the source, believing that small word changes make it their own
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses to copy sentences word for word, or to swap a few words and claim the idea, instead of paraphrasing and naming the source

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student overlooks safe and responsible online conduct when publishing, sharing private information or an unkind tone
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects including a home address and phone number, posting an unkind remark, or sharing a password instead of protecting personal information and keeping a respectful tone

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student believes hunt-and-peck or forceful typing is just as effective as touch typing for producing a multi-page piece
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses one-finger typing while looking at the keys, or hitting keys as hard as possible, instead of home-row touch typing for speed and stamina
